notes.title: The captured Luzon commander and disputed gold
notes.body: Pigafetta reports that the expedition captured a son of Luzon's ruler serving as captain-general of Brunei's ruler and that Giovan Carvalho accepted gold in connection with his release (Robertson's 1906 Ambrosian Italian–English edition, The Philippine Islands, vol. XXXIII, pp. 223–225). The account does not name the prince Ache, identify the payer, or document the novel's dialogue, precise ransom negotiations, list of released people, or the terms of any exchange. Ache's identification is a cross-source historical reconstruction, not Pigafetta's stated name.

notes.title: A later, conflicting release tradition
notes.body: Aganduru Móriz's seventeenth-century narrative says del Cano released the Luzon prince and declined offered gold, contradicting Pigafetta's account of Carvalho accepting gold. Aganduru's Spanish wording has now been directly checked in the indexed text of the 1882 CODOIN vol. 78, printed pp. 59–60; its scanned page images and underlying manuscript remain uncollated. Verification of what this later chronicler wrote does not make his version an eyewitness fact.

notes.title: The captive witnesses and selective release are invented
notes.body: The multilingual sailor, woman in blue, injured younger woman, older mother searching for her swimmer son, boy tending a splinted sailor, junk master seeking his brother, and Ache's particular confinement and release conversations are fictional scene constructions. A separate 1521 document recorded by Martín Méndez reports Carvalho's statement at Tidore on 13 November that three women seized from a Luzon vessel were still held; the 14 November entry records their transfer to Tidore's ruler (1920 published transcription, Document 105, pp. 175–178). That document neither identifies the novel's women nor establishes their eventual freedom or return. The woman in blue asks Ache to report that she was alive but not released; her fictional fate remains unknown.

notes.title: Chronology remains an open source question
notes.body: Pigafetta's 29 July confrontation, Albo's movement outside the harbor and the Genoese pilot's multi-day Roteiro sequence cannot currently be reduced to a single certain day-by-day itinerary. The novel places Ache's release and return before evening while a foreign hull remains visible. That staging is fictional and remains under historical review, especially against the Roteiro's conflicting sequence. The Portuguese Roteiro is available in a 2025 edited transcription; its archival manuscript variants have not been directly inspected.

notes.title: A contemporaneous account of a next-day capture
notes.body: At Tidore on 13 November 1521, expedition pilot Juan Carvalho told the ruler, in a statement recorded by Martín Méndez, that the Europeans first seized a junk and a prao near Brunei and captured a separate junk carrying a son of Luzon's ruler the following day (1920 transcription of the Libro de las paces y amistades, Document 105, pp. 175–176). This retrospective statement by a participant differs from a strictly same-day reading of Pigafetta's 29 July account; it does not supply an exact departure date or prove the novel's hour-by-hour captivity. The archival folio and printed page images have not been checked.
